learn: An urban community is a city, with many people, tall buildings and busy streets.
A suburban community is near a city, with houses, yards and shopping centres.
A rural community is in the countryside, with farms and open land.
check: A community near a city with houses and yards is...
Farms and open land describe a...
lessons.try: Decide which kind of community you live in and name two clues.

lessons.t: How Communities Are Alike and Different
learn: All communities have homes, workers, schools and ways to travel.
They differ in size, weather, jobs and landforms.
A fishing town by the sea is different from a mountain town.
check: A fishing town is probably near...
lessons.try: Compare your community with one in a book or video.

learn: Communities change over time. New buildings are built and old ones are fixed or torn down.
Roads, schools and parks are added as more people move in.
Old photos show how a community looked long ago.
check: What is added as more people move in?
What shows how a community looked long ago?
lessons.try: Find an old photo of your town online with a grown-up. What changed?

learn: A map has a title, a key, a compass rose and a scale.
The scale shows how distance on the map matches real distance: 1 inch might equal 1 mile.
The compass rose shows north, south, east and west, plus in-between directions like northeast.
check: What shows how map distance matches real distance?
lessons.try: Find the scale on a map and measure the distance between two places.

learn: Some maps have a grid of squares with letters and numbers.
A place might be in square B3: column B, row 3.
Grids help you find places quickly.
check: What do grids help you do?
In square B3, B is the...
lessons.try: Draw a grid map of your room and give each object a square.

learn: A globe is a model of Earth. It is round, like Earth.
The equator is an imaginary line around the middle of Earth. It is hot near the equator.
The North Pole and South Pole are at the top and bottom. They are very cold.
check: An imaginary line around the middle of Earth
Near the equator it is usually...
lessons.try: Find the equator and the North Pole on a globe or map.

learn: The United States has 50 states.
Each state has a capital city where its government meets.
The capital of the whole country is Washington, D.C.
check: How many states are in the United States?
What is the capital of the United States?
What happens in a state capital?
lessons.try: Find your state and its capital on a map.

learn: Landmarks are famous places people visit.
The Grand Canyon is a natural landmark. The Golden Gate Bridge is human-made.
The Mississippi River is one of the longest rivers in North America.
lessons.try: Pick a landmark and draw it.

learn: The country has regions, like the Northeast, the Southwest and the Midwest, with different landforms and weather.
Canada is north of the United States. Mexico is south.
The Atlantic Ocean is to the east and the Pacific Ocean is to the west.
check: Which country is north of the United States?
Which ocean is to the west?
Which country is south of the United States?
lessons.try: On a map, point to Canada, Mexico and both oceans.

learn: Needs are things people must have: food, water, clothing and shelter.
Wants are things people would like but can live without: toys, games, treats.
Families plan to pay for needs first.
lessons.try: Make a two-column list of needs and wants in your house.

learn: Scarcity means there is not enough of something for everyone to have all they want.
Because of scarcity, people make choices.
When you choose one thing, the thing you give up is called the opportunity cost.
check: Not enough for everyone to have all they want
What you give up when you choose
lessons.try: You have money for a book or a ball. Choose one. What is your opportunity cost?

learn: A budget is a plan for spending and saving money.
Saving means keeping some money for later. A bank keeps money safe and can pay interest.
Setting a goal, like saving for a bike, helps you save.
check: A plan for spending and saving
Where can money be kept safe?
lessons.try: Make a simple budget for 10 pretend dollars: spend, save and share.

learn: Producers make goods or provide services.
Consumers buy and use goods and services.
Everyone is a consumer. Many people are also producers at their jobs.
lessons.try: Name something you consumed today and who produced it.

learn: People have jobs to earn money and to help the community.
Some jobs make goods, like a baker or a carpenter. Some provide services, like a dentist or a bus driver.
People need training and skills for many jobs.
check: To earn money and help the community
lessons.try: Interview a grown-up about their job.

learn: Specialising means doing one kind of job very well.
Because people specialise, they trade: a farmer sells food and buys shoes from a shoemaker.
Countries trade too, buying and selling goods across the world.
lessons.try: Look at labels on three things at home. Where were they made?

learn: Most food starts on a farm.
Farmers grow crops like wheat, corn and fruit, and raise animals for milk, eggs and meat.
Some food comes from the sea, caught by fishers.
lessons.try: Pick a food from your kitchen and trace where it came from.

learn: Wheat is grown, harvested, cleaned and ground into flour at a mill.
The flour goes to a bakery where bread is made.
Trucks carry the bread to stores, where families buy it.
check: Where is wheat ground into flour?
lessons.try: Draw the journey of bread in four steps.

learn: Many workers help bring food to your table: farmers, truck drivers, factory workers, grocers and cooks.
Each worker depends on the others.
When we eat, we can thank all the people who helped.
check: Who helps bring food to your table?
Do workers depend on each other?
lessons.try: List five workers who helped make your lunch.

learn: Government is the group of people who make laws and run a community, state or country.
Governments provide services like schools, roads, parks and police and fire departments.
People pay taxes to pay for these services.
check: Makes laws and runs a community
lessons.try: Name three services in your community paid for by taxes.

learn: Local government runs a city or town. A mayor and council lead it.
State government runs a state. A governor leads it.
National government runs the country. The president leads it, and Congress makes laws.
lessons.try: Match each leader to their level: mayor, governor, president.

learn: In the United States, people vote for leaders who make laws.
The Constitution is the plan for the country's government. It protects people's rights.
Courts and judges decide if laws are followed fairly.
check: The plan for the country's government
Who decides if laws are followed fairly?
lessons.try: Hold a class or family vote on a rule. Count the votes.

learn: Rights are freedoms that belong to people, like the right to speak freely.
Responsibilities are things people should do, like following laws and respecting others.
Rights and responsibilities go together.
check: A freedom that belongs to people
Do rights and responsibilities go together?
lessons.try: Name one right you have and one responsibility.

learn: Good citizens treat others with respect, even when they disagree.
Being fair means following the same rules for everyone.
Listening to others' ideas helps solve problems.
check: How do good citizens treat others?
lessons.try: Practise disagreeing kindly: "I see it differently because..."

learn: Citizens help their community by volunteering, recycling and caring for public places.
Even small actions, like picking up litter, make a difference.
Groups can work together on bigger projects, like a food drive.
check: Does picking up litter make a difference?
Collecting food for people in need
lessons.try: Plan one way your family can help your community this month.

learn: Long ago, people walked, rode horses or travelled in wagons and on sailing ships.
Later came trains, cars and aeroplanes.
Today people can cross the country in hours instead of months.
check: How did people travel long ago?
lessons.try: Make a timeline of transportation from horses to planes.

learn: Long ago, people wrote letters that took weeks to arrive.
The telegraph, then the telephone, made talking across distance faster.
Today we use computers and phones to send messages instantly.
check: How did people send messages long ago?
lessons.try: Write a letter to a relative and mail it. How long does it take to arrive?

learn: Primary sources are things from the time, like old letters, photos and diaries.
Secondary sources are written later about the past, like a history book.
Historians use both to learn about long ago.
check: A history book written today about long ago is a...
lessons.try: Look at an old family photo. What does it tell you about the past?

learn: Inventors create new things that change how people live.
Benjamin Franklin experimented with electricity and invented bifocal glasses.
George Washington Carver found hundreds of uses for peanuts and helped farmers care for their soil.
check: George Washington Carver found many uses for...
lessons.try: Think of an invention that would help your family.

learn: Some people worked to make life fairer for everyone.
Harriet Tubman led enslaved people to freedom on the Underground Railroad.
Martin Luther King Jr. worked peacefully so all people would be treated equally. Rosa Parks refused to give up her bus seat and helped change unfair laws.
check: Who led people to freedom on the Underground Railroad?
How did Martin Luther King Jr. work for change?
What did Rosa Parks refuse to give up?
lessons.try: Choose one of these people and tell why they were brave.

learn: People who make a difference often see a problem and decide to help.
They are brave, keep trying and work with others.
Children can make a difference too, by helping others and speaking up for what's right.
check: People who make a difference often...
Which trait helps people make a difference?
lessons.try: Write about one way you could make a difference.
